newsitem.title: UK: London gold barely higher, market lacks enthusiasm.
newsitem.headline: London gold barely higher, market lacks enthusiasm.

text.p: Gold prices nudged slightly higher on Tuesday, but found no real impetus to break out of a $382-$385 price range, dealers said.
Bullion fixed at $383.45 an ounce, compared to $383.30 in the morning and a Monday London close of $382.55/$383.05. Bids were quoted in a tight range, holding up above $382 support.
Comex December gold was up $0.40 at $386.70 an ounce, after trading between $387.00 to $386.40.
"There was a little push up this morning, with people thinking the IMF gold sales wouldn't go through. But then people ran out of ideas," a dealer said.
Palladium, which has been sinking on sluggish industrial demand and steady Russian supplies in recent weeks, fixed at a three-year low of $121.0 an ounce in the afternoon.
The other white industrial metals were also sluggish despite a strong performance by European stock markets following record highs on Wall Street on Monday, dealers said.

Gold prices ignored slightly higher than expected U.S. industrial production data. August industrial output rose 0.5 percent, in line with market expectations. Gold also did not react to news that most district banks in the Federal Reserve System requested a discount rate hike.
The Fed consensus centered around a hike of 25-basis points. Bullion dalers have said that a hike below 50 basis points was unlikely to have much of an effect on the market.
The market was still nervous about the International Monetary Fund's meeting on Wednesday to renew discussions on a plan to sell five million ounces of gold to finance projects.
International monetary sources said late on Monday that the IMF was encountering problems reaching agreement on the sale.
Silver was at $5.06/$5.08, up two cents from the Monday London close. But it ran into trouble around $5.08, underscoring the lack of interest in the precious metals, dealers said.
Palladium was the worst performer in the generally gloomy precious metals complex, fixing the lowest since September 20, 1993, after support at $122 crumbled.
The next level was $120, after which important support came in only around $112, some dealers said.
"There was a lot of selling at the platinum/palladium fix. There's no real reason for it, but the longer they sit at these levels the less enthusiastic people are," a dealer said.
Platinum was $0.90 firmer at $388.00/$389.00, but still vulnerable to downside pressure. Support was around $385-$386.
